articles.body: News Port News Top Right Port of Colombo records growth in transshipment volumes November 24, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email The Port of Colombo handled 6,406,363 TEUs of transshipment cargo between January and October 2026, a 10% increase on the 5,825,909 TEUs recorded in the same period of 2025, or an additional 580,454 TEUs. Growth continued in October itself, when the port handled 680,125 TEUs against 620,830 TEUs in October 2025, a year-on-year rise of 9.6 percent and an extra 59,295 TEUs. Reflecting this sustained growth, Colombo advanced to 20th place among the world’s busiest container ports in the first half of 2026, according to the latest Alphaliner rankings, up from 26th place at the end of 2025. The result strengthens Colombo’s standing as a leading transshipment hub in the Indian Ocean, supported by its strategic location, extensive international shipping connections and continued investment in port infrastructure and terminal capacity. Ongoing expansion and modernisation initiatives are expected to further enhance operational capabilities, accommodate growing container volumes and reinforce the port’s position as a competitive maritime gateway linking major global trade routes. articles.title: Grounded bulker pulled free off French coast
articles.summary: Salvors have successfully refloated the 28,200 dwt bulk carrier Miro G, four days after the ship was driven onto a beach on France’s Atlantic coast. The 2011-built, Malta-flagged bulker was pulled clear of the shoreline at Cap de l’Homy, near Lit-et-Mixe, on Tuesday afternoon by Les Abeilles International’s emergency...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Grounded bulker pulled free off French coast Adis Ajdin November 25, 2026 0 140 1 minute read French Navy French Navy Salvors have successfully refloated the 28,200 dwt bulk carrier Miro G , four days after the ship was driven onto a beach on France’s Atlantic coast. The 2011-built, Malta-flagged bulker was pulled clear of the shoreline at Cap de l’Homy, near Lit-et-Mixe, on Tuesday afternoon by Les Abeilles International’s emergency response tug Abeille Bretagne. The vessel is set to be towed north to Le Verdon, at the mouth of the Gironde estuary, according to Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul, who confirmed that no pollution had been detected. The breakthrough followed days of preparations involving Dutch specialist SMIT Salvage, appointed by the shipowner, Les Abeilles International and experts from the French navy. Salvors took advantage of improving sea conditions and a rising tide, pumping ballast water out of the 169-m-long bulker to reduce its draught before pulling it free using a 1,900-m high-strength synthetic towline. Shallow waters had prevented the tug from approaching within about 900 m of the stranded vessel. As reported by Splash on Monday, the Miro G ran aground early on Friday after gusts of up to 48 knots caused it to drag its anchors. The ship was sailing in ballast towards Rouen. Nineteen of the vessel’s 22 crew were airlifted to safety on Friday, with the remaining three evacuated alongside salvage personnel on Saturday ahead of deteriorating weather. articles.title: Used Supertankers Now Cost More Than New Ships as Hormuz War Upends Shipping Markets
articles.summary: The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on immediately available shipping capacity. Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH revealed Tuesday in its third-quarter earnings report that the market value of a 15-year-old very large crude carrier (VLCC) has reached $165 million, some 25% above the $132 million price of ordering a new vessel, according to Clarksons data. The valuation is more than three-and-a-half times the 10-year average of $46 million for a tanker of that age. While newbuildings ordered today may take years to deliver, existing vessels can immediately capitalize on some of the highest tanker freight rates ever recorded. The unusual price inversion underscores how the war has fundamentally altered the economics of moving oil out of the Middle East. A Growing Capacity Crunch Although Middle Eastern oil exports have recovered substantially since the early months of the conflict, the shipping industry is relying on increasingly inefficient arrangements to move crude through the Strait of Hormuz. Combined oil exports from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Qatar reached 10.9 million barrels per day in October, up from 6.7 million barrels per day in April. However, much of that recovery has been facilitated by shuttle voyages and ship-to-ship transfers in the relatively safer waters of the Gulf of Oman. CMB.TECH estimates that 141 tankers are now dedicated exclusively to shuttling crude and petroleum products, with VLCCs accounting for 72% of those vessels. However, according to the CMB.TECH, the number of vessels deployed for shuttling only partly explains why tanker tonnage has become so tight. “A key additional factor is waiting time, with average round voyages extending to 23 days compared with an optimal 9 to 10 days,” the company said. The arrangement effectively removes significant tanker capacity from the wider international market, even as the global fleet continues to grow. The resulting shortage has spilled into other trading regions, driving up freight rates far beyond the Middle East as charterers compete for available tonnage. Unprecedented Earnings CMB.TECH’s Euronav tanker division reported average VLCC spot earnings of $149,945 per day in the third quarter, compared with $30,486 per day a year earlier. So far in the fourth quarter, those earnings have climbed to an extraordinary $635,199 per day, with 59% of available vessel days booked. The company’s Suezmax fleet is also benefiting, securing fourth-quarter spot earnings averaging $377,164 per day, with 68% of available days booked. The booming market has prompted CMB.TECH to capitalize on soaring vessel valuations. The company reported third-quarter net profit of $373.9 million, compared with $17.3 million a year earlier, including $100.2 million in gains from the sale of two Suezmax tankers. Three additional tanker sales are expected to generate approximately $190.8 million in gains during the fourth quarter. A Growing Risk of Reversal The extraordinary market conditions are also encouraging investment in new tanker capacity. The global VLCC orderbook now stands at 33.1% of the existing fleet, while the Suezmax orderbook has reached 29.3%, according to Clarksons data presented by CMB.TECH. An eventual normalization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could release significant tanker capacity back into the international market, potentially coinciding with a wave of newbuilding deliveries in the coming years. Until then, however, CMB.TECH expects the availability of vessels, rather than underlying oil demand, to remain the primary driver of crude tanker earnings. For now, the fact that a 15-year-old supertanker commands a $33 million premium over a new vessel illustrates just how valuable existing shipping capacity has become in a world at war. articles.title: Maersk introduces document amendment fee in North America
articles.summary: Maersk will introduce a Transport Document Amendment Fee for certain shipments loading from ports in the United States and Canada. The charge will take effect on 1 January 2027. A fee of US$75 will apply to eligible amendment requests submitted three or more calendar days after the containers have been loaded aboard...
articles.body: Rates & Surcharges Top Right Maersk introduces document amendment fee in North America November 24, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Maersk will introduce a Transport Document Amendment Fee for certain shipments loading from ports in the United States and Canada. The charge will take effect on 1 January 2027. A fee of US$75 will apply to eligible amendment requests submitted three or more calendar days after the containers have been loaded aboard the vessel at the first load port. Maersk refers to the new timeframe as the “Laden on Board + 3 Day Rule”. The fee will cover late changes to transport document details, including requests to change the document type from a negotiable Bill of Lading to a Sea Waybill or vice versa. Amendments excluded from the fee The charge will not apply to: Seal number additions or modifications Mandatory reference changes required for regulatory or compliance purposes House Bill of Lading requests, amendments or cancellations Out-of-gauge shipments Maersk noted that the fee may still apply when a single request combines an excluded amendment with other chargeable document changes. Customers submitting eligible requests through Maersk.com will be able to view the applicable fee, select the payer and payment terms, and accept the relevant conditions before completing the submission. articles.title: African expansion on the cards for Eco Wave Power with potential 100 MW development
articles.summary: Eco Wave Power is exploring a potential 100 MW wave energy initiative in Africa, following its South African feasibility study.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects November 24, 2026 · 1 minute ago African expansion on the cards for Eco Wave Power with potential 100 MW development Eco Wave Power is exploring a potential 100 MW wave energy initiative in Africa, following its South African feasibility study. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Eco Wave Power Israel-headquartered developer Eco Wave Power has set its sights on a potential expansion in Africa, after its U.S. subsidiary received a letter of intent (LOI) from an African electricity utility to explore up to 100 MW of wave energy capacity, building on its feasibility study in South Africa, which identified approximately 8.3 MW of potential wave energy capacity. Eco Wave Power’s U.S. subsidiary has received a letter of intent from an electricity utility in Africa regarding the proposed exploration and development of up to 100 MW of wave energy capacity. The LOI expresses interest in evaluating wave energy as a means of diversifying electricity sources, strengthening energy security and increasing renewable energy's contribution to the electricity supply. The company, which has not disclosed the utility's identity and the proposed project location at this stage, explains that the initiative represents a significant potential expansion of its activities in Africa, building on the firm's completed feasibility study for approximately 8.3 MW of potential wave energy capacity at South Africa's Port of Ngqura. Eco Wave Power and the undisclosed utility are now expected to advance discussions regarding a proposed feasibility study to assess suitable locations, wave resources, and generation potential, technical and environmental considerations, grid integration, commercial viability, preliminary capital and operating costs, opportunities for local workforce participation and a phased implementation roadmap. " This letter of intent represents an exciting opportunity to build on our progress in Africa and explore the potential for up to 100 MW of wave energy capacity. Our work at South Africa's Port of Ngqura provided valuable experience in evaluating how existing marine infrastructure could support wave energy generation. We now have an opportunity to apply that experience to a substantially larger proposed initiative. " — Inna Braverman Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Eco Wave Power The company emphasizes that the utility indicated its readiness to meet with the company’s U.S. subsidiary for further discussions regarding the proposed initiative. The potential scale of up to 100 MW reflects the duo's interest in evaluating a substantial wave energy opportunity. The proposed feasibility study would determine whether, where, and in what phases that capacity could be technically and commercially viable. Eco Wave Power's technology is designed to generate electricity from ocean and sea waves using floaters attached to coastal structures, with energy conversion equipment located onshore. The proposed assessment would examine opportunities to apply this approach at suitable sites. Eco Wave Power first entered the African market in July 2025 through an agreement with Africa Great Future Development Ltd. (AGFDL) to conduct a feasibility study for a potential wave energy project at the Port of Ngqura in South Africa. Related Articles Marine Energy Eco Wave Power to assess wave energy potential in South Africa 2 min read The firm announced the completion of that study in February 2026, with findings indicating the technical potential to deploy approximately 8.3 MW of installed wave energy capacity along the port's existing breakwater infrastructure, subject to further development and permitting assessments. According to Eco Wave Power, the new LOI represents its second significant step into the African market and an opportunity to evaluate its technology at a substantially larger potential scale. The proposed feasibility study is expected to provide the foundation for assessing the initiative's technical, economic and environmental viability and identifying possible phases for future development. Our ambition is to turn that resource into productive energy infrastructure, generating clean electricity close to the communities and industries that need it. We look forward to advancing discussions with the utility and defining a rigorous feasibility study to assess suitable sites, commercial potential and a phased path toward possible deployment. " — Braverman added. The firm points out that the initiative remains subject to completion of feasibility and technical assessments, agreement on project scope, and commercial terms, execution of definitive agreements, applicable regulatory and permitting approvals, and appropriate project financing. The LOI does not constitute a definitive agreement to construct or purchase a 100 MW project, and there can be no assurance that the initiative will proceed or reach the contemplated capacity. Eco Wave Power, which developed and operates Israel's first grid-connected wave energy power station, recently launched the first-ever onshore wave energy pilot station in the United States at the Port of Los Angeles, in collaboration with Shell Marine Renewable Energy. The company is expanding globally with projects planned in Portugal , Taiwan , and India , representing a project pipeline of up to 504.7 MW. articles.title: Seatrium to cut Singapore workforce as it consolidates shipyards
articles.summary: Singapore-based marine engineering group Seatrium has announced plans to reduce approximately 2% of its Singapore workforce as part of a restructuring programme aimed at improving operational efficiency and aligning resources with future projects. The announcement, made on 24 November 2026, marks the company’s first...
articles.body: Singapore-based marine engineering group Seatrium has announced plans to reduce approximately 2% of its Singapore workforce as part of a restructuring programme aimed at improving operational efficiency and aligning resources with future projects. The announcement, made on 24 November 2026, marks the company’s first workforce restructuring exercise since its merger in 2023. The programme will also accelerate the consolidation of Seatrium’s shipyard operations in Singapore and support a more integrated global operating model. Seatrium said its worldwide yard network has already been reduced from 15 facilities in 2023 to 11. Singapore shipyards to undergo further changes Under the restructuring, Tuas Boulevard Yard will remain Seatrium’s flagship mega-yard, while Admiralty Yard will continue to be scaled down ahead of its planned return to the Singapore Government in 2028. The group’s other Singapore facilities, Benoi Yard, Pioneer Yard and Tuas Yard, will focus more closely on projects that best match their operational capabilities. In particular, Tuas Yard will shift towards higher-value vessel repairs and upgrades. These changes form part of the One Seatrium Global Delivery Model, which coordinates the company’s international shipyard network from Singapore. The model is intended to improve capacity utilisation and allow projects to be assigned to the most suitable facilities. Workforce reduction follows operational review Seatrium said it reviewed redeployment opportunities, employee training and other workforce measures before deciding to eliminate certain positions. Approximately 2% of its Singapore workforce will be affected by the restructuring. “Our people have been instrumental in building Seatrium into the global business it is today, and we are deeply grateful for every colleague’s contributions over the past 60 years,” said Chris Ong, Chief Executive Officer of Seatrium. “We are not downsizing or simply cost cutting. We are repositioning and readying Seatrium to capture new opportunities,” Ong added. The company said it invested approximately S$7 million in employee training during 2025 and delivered more than 600,000 training hours globally. Seatrium Employees Union (SEU) was informed of the restructuring in advance and has worked with the company to support affected employees. The union said the assistance would include outplacement support and access to employment services through Singapore’s labour movement. Seatrium expects the restructuring to proceed without disruption to ongoing operations or project execution. The company has not disclosed the exact number of affected employees or the financial savings expected from the programme.

articles.summary: ExxonMobil’s final investment decision (FID) will extend production at Block 15 fields, while a new discovery marks the block’s 21st hydrocarbon find.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 24, 2026 · 3 minutes ago ExxonMobil signs off on $4 billion FID as new discovery signals more oil potential at Angolan offshore block ExxonMobil’s final investment decision (FID) will extend production at Block 15 fields, while a new discovery marks the block’s 21st hydrocarbon find. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Valaris DS-9 drillship Source: ExxonMobil U.S.-headquartered energy giant ExxonMobil and its partners have committed $4 billion to a life extension project in Block 15 off the coast of Angola, as a new hydrocarbon discovery reinforces the untapped potential at the same block, strengthening prospects for sustained offshore production and renewed investment. ExxonMobil and the Block 15 partners have formalized a final investment decision estimated at $4 billion for the redevelopment of Kizomba A , Kizomba B , and the development of the Likembe field , concluding the FID of the Block 15 Life Extension project , following the approval of the Kizomba C redevelopment in 2025, according to Angola’s National Agency of Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG) . This life extension project is expected to benefit from existing infrastructure and develop additional resources throughout the Kizomba Pole area. ANPG and the ExxonMobil-operated contractor group have also disclosed a new discovery in the Tchihumba West-01ST1 exploration well. The latest find is the 21st discovery in Block 15 and the second one this year, which ANPG believes is a demonstration of the significant remaining resource potential in the offshore block. The Tchihumba West-01ST1 exploration well encountered a 65.4-meter sandstone reservoir containing hydrocarbons and exhibiting good petrophysical properties. " The formalization of the final investment decision for the redevelopment of Kizomba A and B, associated with the new hydrocarbon discovery in the Tchihumba West-01ST1 well, constitutes an important milestone for the national oil industry and attests to the exploratory potential that still exists in Angola's mature producing fields. " — Paulino Jerónimo Chairman of the Board of Directors of ANPG The well is located approximately 350 kilometers northwest of Luanda and was drilled by the Valaris DS-9 rig in a water depth of around 1,400 meters. The approval of the Kizomba A and Kizomba B redevelopment projects, along with the discovery of Tchihumba West-01ST1, supports the continuity of production and highlights the role of investment, technology, and exploration in developing Angola's significant offshore resource base. " Through strategic investment, technology and exploration, we continue to maximize the recovery of existing resources and identify new development opportunities. With the support of the extension of the production sharing agreement for Block 15 until 2037 and approximately $4 billion in planned new investments, including the development of the Likembe field and the activities of the Block 15 Life Extension project, we are well positioned to continue generating value for Angola, our partners and our shareholders. " — Brian Unietis ExxonMobil's Managing Director Another oil project offshore Angola is making headaway in its development, as confirmed by a visit TotalEnergies, Petronas, Sonangol, and ANPG made overseas to check on the construction of critical subsea equipment for the African project. articles.summary: Greek containership owner Danaos has secured another $611m in contracted revenue through a string of new fixtures and charter extensions, taking its forward revenue backlog to $5bn. articles.body: Containers Europe Danaos bags $611m in fresh boxship charters Adis Ajdin November 24, 2026 0 204 1 minute read Danaos Danaos Greek containership owner Danaos has secured another $611m in contracted revenue through a string of new fixtures and charter extensions, taking its forward revenue backlog to $5bn. The John Coustas-led company revealed the deals in its latest quarterly update, with a comparison of its fleet employment schedules showing fresh contracts for six containership newbuildings alongside longer employment for several ships already on the water. Four 5,300 teu vessels ordered at CSSC’s Huangpu Wenchong Shipyard earlier this year have secured three-year charters. The quartet, scheduled for delivery in 2028 and 2029, was previously listed without employment. Another two 9,000 teu newbuildings booked in September for delivery in early 2029 have secured charters running for at least 4.8 years. Danaos has also extended employment coverage for three of its largest containerships, the 2012-built, 13,100 teu Kota Plumbago, Kota Primrose and Kota Peony , from 2027 into 2029. The latest fixtures leave just two of the New York-listed owner’s 28 containership newbuildings without disclosed charter commitments. Both are 1,800 teu feeders scheduled for delivery in 2028 and 2029. Danaos has now covered 94% of its available containership operating days for next year, 84% for 2028 and 71% for 2029. More than half of its 2030 capacity is also contracted. The company previously disclosed $683m in additional charter revenue in August. Meanwhile, Danaos has formally confirmed it is putting plans for a separate Norwegian listing of its dry bulk business on hold, a move previously reported by Splash in October. The AThens-based owner controls 78 containerships totalling more than 502,000 teu, alongside 11 capesizes. Its newbuilding programme includes 28 boxships and four 211,000 dwt newcastlemax bulkers. articles.title: ShipVet Appoints New CEO as Founder Steps Back
articles.summary: Marine assurance and vessel vetting company ShipVet has appointed James Stairmand as chief executive officer, effective November 2026, as founder Captain Fintan Cullen moves to a non-executive role.Stairmand, previously the company's chief commercial officer…
articles.body: ShipVet Appoints New CEO as Founder Steps Back Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 James Stairmand (Credit: ShipVet) Marine assurance and vessel vetting company ShipVet has appointed James Stairmand as chief executive officer, effective November 2026, as founder Captain Fintan Cullen moves to a non-executive role. Stairmand, previously the company's chief commercial officer, joined ShipVet as part of a management buy-in in late 2024, backed by Frontier Development Capital. Since the investment, ShipVet has expanded its vessel vetting team with specialists from major oil companies, rebuilt its digital platform and strengthened its sanctions screening capabilities. The company's platform supports vessel assessments and sanctions screening, with maritime specialists evaluating the findings against clients' vetting policies and providing recommendations. Stairmand has more than 20 years of experience in the commodities sector and previously founded, expanded and exited OnlineFuels, a digital marketplace for downstream fuels. Cullen, who founded ShipVet in 1997, will remain involved with the company as a non-executive director. Headquartered in London, ShipVet provides independent vessel vetting and marine assurance services to the oil, gas and commodities sectors, including vessel suitability assessments, vetting policy design and sanctions screening. “Charterers need to understand the risks associated with a vessel and how those risks relate to their own requirements. Our job is to provide a clear assessment and be available to discuss it. “Fintan has built a business that clients trust. Since the buy-in, we have invested in the expertise and technology needed to develop that service further. My focus as CEO is to bring it to more charterers while preserving the judgement and responsiveness that have underpinned ShipVet’s work,” said James Stairmand, Chief Executive Officer of ShipVet.

articles.body: The Port of Gothenburg is installing overhead line infrastructure on the container terminal’s handling tracks, allowing electric locomotives to run directly to and from the terminal. This removes the need for diesel locomotives or detours via the port departure yard, and is intended to raise capacity, cut emissions and make rail operations more efficient. Construction is due to begin next year. The terminal is operated by APM Terminals and handles about 80 trains a week, linking the port with more than 20 destinations across Sweden. Rail freight is growing: a record 529,000 TEU moved to and from the port by rail last year, and volumes have continued to rise in 2026. The project aims to make better use of existing infrastructure as demand increases. The investment is expected to shorten total turnaround times for container rail shuttles by up to 30 minutes, because trains can depart straight from the terminal rather than spending time in the departure yard. It will also improve handling of trains of up to 750 metres, whereas train length is currently limited by the 630-metre tracks in the departure yard. The scope includes about 1,250 metres of overhead line, 38 line masts with foundations, upgraded level crossing protection systems and a new emergency access road, improving safety and resilience for both road and rail traffic. Birna Ödefors, Managing Director of APM Terminals Gothenburg, said that electrifying the final stretch removes another fossil fuel dependency from the transport flow, giving customers better opportunities to cut emissions and strengthening rail as a sustainable and competitive option. Robert Sommar, Railway Manager at the Port of Gothenburg, said more efficient traffic arrangements will create better conditions for both growth and sustainable transport.
takeaways: The Port of Gothenburg is installing overhead line infrastructure on the container terminal’s handling tracks, allowing electric locomotives to run directly to and from the terminal.
This removes the need for diesel locomotives or detours via the port departure yard, and is intended to raise capacity, cut emissions and make rail operations more efficient.
Construction is due to begin next year.

articles.body: Europe Offshore EnEarth takes control of Scottish carbon storage project Bojan Lepic November 24, 2026 0 149 1 minute read EnEarth EnEarth Carbon storage developer EnEarth has agreed to acquire Storegga’s 30% stake in the Acorn carbon capture and storage project in northeast Scotland, taking over as lead developer of the North Sea scheme. The transaction will transfer Storegga’s project interest and development responsibilities to EnEarth, together with the management team and staff currently working on Acorn. The acquisition is expected to be completed before the end of 2026, subject to the necessary approvals. Financial terms have not been disclosed. Acorn is being developed around the St Fergus gas terminal near Peterhead and is designed to transport captured industrial carbon dioxide for permanent storage in depleted offshore gas reservoirs. The project includes the Acorn and East Mey offshore storage areas, which have estimated combined storage capacity exceeding 140m tonnes of CO2. Once developed, the facilities are expected to inject between 5m and 10m tonnes of CO2 annually into reservoirs approximately 2.5 km beneath the seabed. EnEarth, which was established by Greek oil and gas producer Energean, is also developing the Prinos CO2 storage project in Greece and pursuing carbon storage opportunities elsewhere in southeastern Europe. The acquisition follows Storegga’s decision last year to review its business and seek a buyer for its Acorn interest. The project has faced uncertainty over funding and the pace of UK government support, with a final investment decision still outstanding. EnEarth aims to progress the development towards commercial sanction, with potential operations beginning in the early 2030s. U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard has sought a specialized salvage inspection of the damaged No. 2 diesel generator aboard USCGC Healy , seeking to identify components that can be reclaimed and reused following a catastrophic engine failure. The procurement goes well beyond a conventional engine repair contract. The Coast Guard’s October 21 statement of work calls for a comprehensive, component-by-component assessment of the damaged Sulzer 12ZAV40S engine, including measurements against allowable clearances, an evaluation of component wear and identification of parts suitable for reclamation and reuse. The contractor must document its findings in a comprehensive report with high-resolution color photographs. The Coast Guard announced its intent to award the work on a sole-source basis to Virginia-based Defense Maritime Solutions. The inspection was scheduled for October 26–30 at Coast Guard Base Seattle. The solicitation also included an optional work item, capped at $100,000, to inspect, repair and requalify the engine’s camshaft. The documents do not establish whether that option was exercised or what the inspection ultimately found. The work follows the July casualty, when Healy suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of its No. 2 main propulsion diesel generator while operating northwest of Port Angeles, Washington. The vessel was towed to Seattle on July 13. Related procurement documents describe a fire in Generator Room No. 2 that exposed fire-detection equipment and wiring to high temperatures, causing a ground fault and requiring extensive replacement work. The casualty disrupted the cutter’s planned Arctic summer deployment . The Coast Guard has also been addressing maintenance requirements on engines No. 1 and No. 3. A separate October procurement sought overhaul of their governors and overspeed protection equipment. Both governors had accumulated more than 40,000 operating hours, with no documented service or overhaul history. The work also called for replacing a damaged cylinder head on engine No. 3. The removed head and dummy valve were to be sent to a machine shop for inspection and reconditioning in accordance with original equipment manufacturer specifications. The Coast Guard specified cylinder head part number 107.122.903.200, National Stock Number 2815-01-465-2075. Separately, supply-chain database records for the part list no active suppliers and indicate that the government does not hold the technical-data rights needed to have alternative manufacturers reproduce it using the proprietary data. The database’s acquisition guidance calls for purchasing directly from the actual manufacturer. This does not establish that the part is unavailable, but it could limit alternative sourcing options if the original manufacturer cannot supply it . “Most of the machinery systems aboard are antiquated and for some there aren’t even parts,” Vice Commandant of the Coast Guard Admiral Kevin E. Lunday said previously following a fire aboard Healy in 2024. Engine challenges are not entirely new for Healy . In 2020, a fire damaged the ship’s starboard propulsion motor, forcing it to abandon an Arctic deployment . The Coast Guard replaced the motor with a spare that had been stored at the Coast Guard Yard in Baltimore for 23 years. Moving the roughly 100-ton unit to a California shipyard required a barge voyage through the Panama Canal and removal of part of the ship’s hull for installation. The latest procurement records do not establish whether the No. 2 diesel generator can be returned to service or which of its components can be recovered. They do, however, show the Coast Guard undertaking a detailed salvage assessment and highlight potential parts-sourcing challenges across the remaining propulsion plant. KYIV, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Ukraine’s foreign minister said on Tuesday a drone attack against a Russian military vessel and cargo ship in Libyan waters at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defense, following criticism from the government in Tripoli. Andrii Sybiha said that both Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment were valid targets and Ukraine’s right to self-defense was enshrined in the United Nations charter, Article 51. Libya’s Tripoli-based Government of National Unity condemned on Monday the Ukrainian military operation that sank the Russian naval corvette Merkury in the eastern port of Benghazi. It said Libya would not accept being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Benghazi is controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army has ties with Russia. The internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli controls western Libya. “Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere,” Sybiha said on the Telegram messaging app. “Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine’s actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people.” International law does not limit the right to self-defense to the territory where the aggression takes place: it can be on the territory of the aggressor, or in international waters, Sybiha said. Russia, he said, was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastructure for its military purposes. The Institute for the Study of War said the Russian naval corvette had stopped over for several days at Benghazi port to refuel and resupply, under a cooperation agreement, as it escorted cargo ships that can carry military supplies to Russia. The eastern government in Benghazi on Monday said there were indications the naval drones were launched from western Libya and asked the UN to investigate allegations that Ukraine has deployed military experts there. Russia’s defense minister has not commented publicly on the attack. In an interview published on Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for a separate drone strike on Saturday on a Russian cargo vessel in the international waters of the Gulf of Finland. He said the vessel, Sparta II, was a legitimate target because it was carrying weapons. The damaged vessel was towed back to the Russian port of St Petersburg, Russia’s Transport Ministry said on Tuesday. The vessels are designed to transport LPG and ammonia and incorporate fuel-saving technologies. articles.title: Torvald Klaveness puts $7bn price tag on shipping inefficiencies
articles.summary: Norwegian shipping group Torvald Klaveness has identified around $7bn in potential annual savings across dry bulk and product tanker shipping, with excessive transaction costs, underutilised vessels and poor port coordination among the industry’s biggest sources of inefficiency. The Oslo-based company’s new study,...
articles.body: Bunkering Dry Cargo Operations Ports and Logistics Tankers Torvald Klaveness puts $7bn price tag on shipping inefficiencies Adis Ajdin November 24, 2026 0 348 2 minutes read Torvald Klaveness Torvald Klaveness Norwegian shipping group Torvald Klaveness has identified around $7bn in potential annual savings across dry bulk and product tanker shipping, with excessive transaction costs, underutilised vessels and poor port coordination among the industry’s biggest sources of inefficiency. The Oslo-based company’s new study, examining approximately $190bn in annual freight spending across the two sectors, suggests the wider opportunity could be worth between $10bn and $20bn a year. The research examined around 50 potential sources of inefficiency, with 14 investigated in detail using voyage data, market benchmarks and operational evidence. At the top of the list is an estimated $1.6bn in avoidable transaction costs, reflecting commercial arrangements where charges are linked to freight and time-charter values rather than improvements in efficiency. Another $1.4bn could be unlocked by deploying larger vessels on trades currently served by smaller ships, while better use of available cargo capacity represents a further $1bn opportunity. Port inefficiencies also feature prominently. Klaveness calculates that around $700m could potentially be saved by improving vessel arrival times, reducing the practice of ships steaming at higher speeds only to wait at anchor for a berth. The study examined approximately 429,000 dry bulk port calls during 2025, identifying around 16,000 cases involving vessels that had sailed for at least seven days before spending three or more days waiting. The wider utilisation figures are equally revealing. Capesize bulkers spent just 40% of their on-hire days sailing laden during 2025, compared with 33% in ballast and another 12% waiting in port. Klaveness also identified around $400m in potential fuel savings from addressing misaligned incentives in time-charter contracts, where shipowners may have limited financial motivation to invest in efficiency improvements because charterers pay for the fuel. Other costs include an estimated $300m from claims and disputes, while unreliable shipping schedules could be adding between $300m and $700m annually to the financing costs of excess inventories held by dry bulk importers. The study, conducted over nearly four months with independent adviser Cardo Partners, draws on Klaveness’s internal voyage database alongside external market data. It puts annual freight spending at approximately $140bn for dry bulk and $50bn for product tankers, with the identified inefficiencies spanning commercial contracting, vessel deployment, port operations and cargo owners’ working capital. Ernst Meyer, chief executive of Torvald Klaveness, argued that the problem lies less with individual companies than with the way shipping’s commercial interests are structured. “Every party is acting rationally, but the incentives don’t line up,” Meyer said. Klaveness noted that better coordination between cargo owners, charterers, operators, shipowners and ports, supported by improved data and artificial intelligence, could unlock much of the value currently being lost. The group has already been pursuing trading efficiency through its dry bulk operations, combination carriers and digital business, including tools designed to improve cargo planning and commercial decisions. Klaveness cautioned that the $7bn figure represents an indicative sum of potential savings rather than a net savings forecast, with some overlap between individual estimates. A further $3bn in opportunities has been identified but not yet quantified, while the broader $10bn to $20bn range includes potential savings that remain unexplored. articles.body: cargo-partner has announced further changes to its European operations as it strengthens its role within Nippon Express Holdings (NX Group), with a particular focus on Central and Eastern Europe. Under the revised structure, cargo-partner will remain a distinct logistics business within NX Group, concentrating on markets where it has an established presence and infrastructure. The company expects to operate in more than 20 countries in 2027, forming a specialised Central and Eastern European logistics network within the wider group. Changes planned across European markets The latest restructuring builds on the integration of Nippon Express operations into cargo-partner businesses in Austria, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia. In the Czech Republic, cargo-partner will complete its transition to NX cargo-partner on 1 January 2027, bringing the regional operations under a unified structure. A different approach will apply in Western Europe. During 2027, cargo-partner operations in the United Kingdom and Ireland will move fully under the Nippon Express brand. The company said the changes are intended to align resources more closely with the strengths of each business and improve operational efficiency. Central and Eastern Europe will remain cargo-partner’s primary regional focus, with Budapest and Vienna serving as important air freight hubs. The company will also continue using the ports of Koper and Rijeka to support trade connections between the region and international markets, particularly Asia. Luca Ferrara takes additional role at NX Group Alongside the operational changes, cargo-partner CEO Luca Ferrara has been appointed Associate Director of Global Network Development at Nippon Express Holdings. The appointment will take effect on 1 January 2027. Ferrara will retain his position as CEO of cargo-partner while taking on additional responsibilities for developing and aligning international network initiatives across NX Group. “Over the past three years, our roadmap with Nippon Express has advanced with consistency and discipline,” said Luca Ferrara, CEO of cargo-partner. “Our integration model proves that preserving specialized local expertise while leveraging an unmatched global asset base delivers the highest value to our clients,” Ferrara added. cargo-partner joined NX Group in January 2024 and has since been integrating its operations with the Japanese logistics group across several markets. The company said it has achieved its financial and business targets for 2026, although the announcement did not provide detailed figures. The latest changes are intended to establish a clearer division of responsibilities between cargo-partner and Nippon Express while supporting international freight forwarding operations across the combined network.

articles.body: Asia Europe Offshore Indonesia clears offshore gas development for Eni-Petronas venture Bojan Lepic November 24, 2026 0 431 1 minute read Eni Eni Indonesian authorities have approved the development plan for the Geliga gas field offshore East Kalimantan, paving the way for a major new deepwater production hub involving an FPSO vessel and 15 subsea wells. The approval, announced by Italian energy major Eni, covers the integrated development of Geliga and neighbouring Gula in the Kutei Basin, containing an estimated 8.1 trillion cubic feet of gas in place. Geliga, discovered earlier this year, holds approximately 5.9 tcf of gas and 250m barrels of associated condensate in place, while Gula contains another 2.2 tcf of gas. Searah, the joint venture established in June by Eni and Malaysia’s Petronas, will operate the project. The development calls for 15 subsea wells connected to a newbuild FPSO capable of processing around 1bn cubic feet of gas and 80,000 barrels of condensate per day, with storage capacity of approximately 1.4m barrels. Peak production is expected to reach 1bn cubic feet of gas and 50,000 barrels of condensate per day. Gas will be exported through the Santan Terminal and East Kalimantan pipeline network, supplying domestic customers and the Bontang LNG plant. According to Indonesian regulator SKK Migas, the development plan was approved just six months after Geliga’s discovery, with first production targeted for 2029. The project will become the third major gas production hub in the Kutei Basin, alongside the producing South Hub and the North Hub development sanctioned in March. The North Hub involves 16 subsea wells tied to another newbuild FPSO and is expected to start production in 2028. Eni recently brought the Maha gas field onstream, connecting two subsea wells to the existing Jangkrik floating production unit. With the three hubs, Eni expects gross production in East Kalimantan to reach about 3bn cubic feet of gas and 140,000 barrels of condensate per day by the end of the decade. No FPSO construction or subsea installation contracts have been announced for Geliga/Gula, which has yet to reach a final investment decision. articles.body: Europe Operations One Maritime Generation targets specialist shipmanagement niche Sam Chambers November 24, 2026 0 340 1 minute read Two German shipping professionals from markedly different maritime backgrounds have established a shipmanagement company in Hamburg, targeting a niche in the market for vessels engaged in complex and unconventional operations. One Maritime Generation brings together Gerda Rohden, a veteran of German family-owned shipping, and Anna-Maria Renken, a qualified lawyer whose maritime career spans commercial shipping, offshore operations, ocean racing and humanitarian search-and-rescue missions. Registered in Hamburg, the company is looking to build a business providing third-party shipmanagement services, with vessels operated by non-governmental organisations (NGOs) among its target markets. Rohden comes from a shipping family whose shipmanagement activities date back to 1959. She was also previously involved in the management of Liberty Blue Shipmanagement. Renken brings more than a decade of international maritime experience, combining legal expertise with practical knowledge of vessel acquisitions, technical management, flag state requirements and classification. The new venture’s services encompass technical and operational management, procurement, financial reporting, insurance, regulatory compliance and crewing support. The company is placing particular emphasis on developing a “no-blame culture”, encouraging employees to identify and address operational shortcomings without fear of repercussions. Its focus on humanitarian and other specialist vessels differentiates the business from many established third-party shipmanagers, with such operations often presenting unusual regulatory, insurance and crewing challenges that require expertise extending beyond conventional merchant shipping.Moreover, in a segment of shipping where men are almost exclusively picked for the top roles, the founders gender sets this new venture apart. articles.title: Elaine Chao Calls for Investment, Innovation to Rebuild U.S. Maritime Industry
articles.summary: Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao called for a coordinated effort involving government, private industry and international allies to strengthen American shipbuilding capacity, modernize maritime infrastructure and develop the workforce needed to support a more competitive U.S.
articles.body: Elaine Chao Calls for Investment, Innovation to Rebuild U.S. Maritime Industry Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 24, 2026 Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao speaking recently at Webb Institute. Image courtesy Webb Institute Secretary Elaine Chao, 18th U.S. Secretary of Transportation and 24th U.S. Secretary of Labor, received an honorary Doctor of Science degree from Webb Institute. She also joined President Mark Martecchini for a fireside chat on the future of U.S. shipbuilding and the maritime industry. Image courtesy Webb Institute Secretary Elaine Chao visits with Bruce Rosenblatt at Webb Institute. Image courtesy Webb Institute During the visit, Webb conferred an honorary Doctor of Science degree upon Chao in recognition of her public service and contributions to transportation and maritime policy. Image courtesy Webb Institute Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao called for a coordinated effort involving government, private industry and international allies to strengthen American shipbuilding capacity, modernize maritime infrastructure and develop the workforce needed to support a more competitive U.S. maritime industry. Speaking November 16, 2026, at Webb Institute in Glen Cove, N.Y. , Chao outlined the challenges facing the American maritime sector, pointing to the country's diminished commercial shipbuilding capacity and the strategic importance of maintaining a strong domestic maritime industrial base. "More than 80 percent of world trade by volume moves by sea," Chao said, noting that the United States accounts for less than one percent of global large commercial ship construction. "The question isn't whether America should strengthen its maritime capabilities. The question is how." Chao, who served as U.S. Secretary of Transportation from 2017 to 2021 and Secretary of Labor from 2001 to 2009, identified several priorities, including increased public and private investment, advanced shipbuilding technology, workforce development and more resilient supply chains for critical marine equipment. She also emphasized cooperation with trusted international partners, particularly Japan and South Korea, whose shipbuilding industries have significant production capacity and technical expertise. Central to her message was the need to ensure that federal maritime investments deliver measurable industrial and economic benefits. "The objective is not simply to build more ships. It is to create an industry that can compete, innovate, attract investment, and meet the strategic needs for the future," Chao said. NSMV Program Offers a Model Chao pointed to the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel (NSMV) program as an example of how federal investment can support shipbuilding employment while addressing long-term maritime workforce requirements. During her tenure at the Department of Transportation, Chao worked with Congress to secure $900 million for the first three vessels, helping establish the foundation for the five-ship program. The ships are being constructed at Philadelphia Shipyard, where employment grew from approximately 50 workers to more than 1,200 by 2023. Each NSMV can accommodate approximately 600 cadets, providing practical training in navigation, marine engineering, ship operations and safety. The vessels also incorporate emergency response capabilities, including medical facilities, helicopter landing areas and accommodations for approximately 1,000 people during humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations. The program illustrates how government shipbuilding contracts can simultaneously address national security, workforce development and industrial capacity. Developing the Maritime Workforce Chao's remarks came during a significant year for Webb Institute, which was designated a Center of Excellence for Domestic Maritime Workforce Training and Education by the U.S. Maritime Administration in September 2026. Webb, which offers a dual Bachelor of Science degree in Naval Architecture and Marine Engineering, combines classroom education with four Winter Work internships providing students with practical maritime industry experience. During the visit, Webb conferred an honorary Doctor of Science degree upon Chao in recognition of her public service and contributions to transportation and maritime policy.

The PRGT project involves the construction of an approximately 750-kilometre natural gas pipeline connecting gas fields in northeastern British Columbia to the planned Ksi Lisims LNG facility at Wil Milit on Canada's west coast. The pipeline will comprise approximately 700 kilometers of onshore infrastructure and 50 kilometers offshore. The project is being developed by NW Infrastructure Limited Partnership, a joint venture between Western LNG and the Nisga'a Nation. The workforce redesign, announced jointly with the Seatrium Employees Union (SEU) on November 24, marks the company's first workforce restructuring exercise since its merger in 2023. Seatrium said it had reviewed redeployment, employee upskilling and other workforce optimization measures before proceeding with the restructuring. The company invested approximately S$7 million in employee training in 2025 and delivered more than 600,000 training hours globally across technical, leadership and capability-building programs. SEU was notified ahead of the exercise and worked with the company on arrangements for affected employees, including retrenchment packages and outplacement assistance. The union will also provide additional support through labour movement resources, including NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute. articles.title: LNG, bio-LNG carbon values still open a week before IMO net-zero decision: e-NG
articles.summary: The International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee will open the Marine Environment Protection Committee85 meeting on Nov. 30 without final rules on how LNG, bio-LNG and e-LNG are measured under the Net-Zero Framework, leaving the compliance value of those fuels unsettled, according to...
articles.body: LNG, bio-LNG carbon values still open a week before IMO net-zero decision: e-NG in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 The International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee will open the Marine Environment Protection Committee85 meeting on Nov. 30 without final rules on how LNG, bio-LNG and e-LNG are measured under the Net-Zero Framework, leaving the compliance value of those fuels unsettled, according to the e-NG Coalition, an industry group promoting e-methane. Default LNG values remain unsettled Default values, avoided emissions and the use of actual well-to-tank values for fossil fuels were all deferred in full from the 22nd Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 22) in September to ISWG-GHG 23 on Nov. 23-27, Rafik Ammar, policy director at e-NG, said. “This leaves one working week for the two workstreams that determine every fuel’s numerical competitiveness,” he told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. Despite this, initial recommendations from The Joint Group of Experts on the Scientific Aspects of Marine Environmental Protection, or GESAMP, recommended an initial well-to-tank default of 32.1 grams of CO2 equivalent/megajoule for e-LNG made from renewable hydrogen and fossil point-source CO2, against 18 gCO2e/MJ for fossil-based LNG. The figures cover only the well-to-tank stage, and most fossil LNG emissions occur at combustion, while the CO2 released by e-LNG was captured upstream. This negates a carbon capture and utilisation accounting methodology for e-NG, and therefore a complete well-to-wake picture is missing from the methodology, Ammar said. For bio-methane, a default value has yet to be determined, with anaerobic-digestion submissions ranging from 11.6-31.1 gCO2e/MJ. For alignment, GESAMP wants satisfactory values from at least three representative studies first, with the proposed submission of 31.1 gCO2/MJ the only satisfactory submission, Ammar said. Crucially for bio-LNG, net-negative emissions accounting under the IMO Net Zero Framework has not yet been clarified and is still pending, unlike in FuelEU, where negative emissions count towards compliance balance. Additionally, a global mass balancing guideline for grid-based fuels will be submitted in ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85, leaving uncertainty for LNG and bio-LNG producers accordingly. Platts assessments of unsubsidized Rotterdam bio-LNG averaged $2,836.92/metric ton in October, rising 47% from $1,932.35/mt in October 2025. Too late for changes this year Little scope remains to change values this year, with a new value requiring a fresh submission at least 28 weeks before an MEPC and a new GESAMP review, and therefore MEPC 85 is invited to agree or reject the existing report, Ammar said. Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella said in an Aug. 20 statement that any viable proposal “must allow for the maximum range of alternate fuel sources, including LNG and bio-LNG,” which she said could realistically supply over 60% of global maritime fuel by 2050. With no clear accommodation on various LNG fuels within the IMO Net Zero Framework expected, any resolution will likely be for 2027. “I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027, it will be codified,” DiBella told Platts at the IBIA annual convention on Nov. 11. “But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus.” NZF Fund in spotlight A post-examination of the ISWG 22 meeting in September harnessed sentiments from member states for the vote in December, with 59 states backing the existing Net Zero Framework as it is on the basis of MEPC 84, according to an overview report from the UCL Energy Institute published in September. The bigger obstacle under discourse has been the Net Zero Fund, with ‘significant work and deliberation’ required over the purpose and functionality of the Fund as a financial mechanism, Ammar told Platts. Despite this, UCL counted 38 states in favor of a fund, facility or similar structure and 17 against among those that spoke at ISWG-GHG 22, and pointed to adjusted design, such as softer early greenhouse gas fuel intensity limits, as likelier than removal. Increasing favourability towards adjustments in the GHG intensity levels for more lenient carbon intensity requirements initially is just one example of how any potential Net Zero Framework outcome in December will likely be one that differs from ‘as is’ as a form of compromise. “Instinctively, all parties want to reach a deal today, with some preferring the existing and others a watered-down version,” Joey Ng, Global Head of Decarbonization at shipping company Braemar, told Platts. “What has shifted since 2025 is the increasing detachment from the initial principles and the shift towards politics instead of science.” Source: Platts 2026-11-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: How chokepoint disruption reshapes maritime risk
articles.summary: Around 90% of world trade travels by sea, much of it through a relatively small number of narrow maritime passages. articles.body: How chokepoint disruption reshapes maritime risk in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 Around 90% of world trade travels by sea, much of it through a relatively small number of narrow maritime passages. For shipowners, operators and marine insurers, the risks around those chokepoints are familiar. What is harder to judge is how quickly disruption at one can change conditions elsewhere. Conflict has disturbed established routes over the past two years, while drought has put pressure on infrastructure that global supply chains depend on. Ships wait, divert or change schedules, with the effects often reaching far beyond the original point of disruption. Recent Pole Star Global research, using Pole Star Global Zone Traffic data from nine major chokepoints between January 2024 and September 2026, gives a sense of the scale. To provide a like-for-like comparison, the percentage changes compare average daily transits from January to August in each year. Among the clearest shifts, average daily transits through the Strait of Hormuz were 64.9% lower between January and August 2026, than over the same period in 2024. Bosporus Strait traffic rose by 176.5% on the same comparison, while Panama Canal traffic was 28.2% higher. Taken together, the figures show how disruption at one major route can reshape traffic and risk elsewhere in the network. Saleem Khan, Chief Data & Analytics Officer, Pole Star Global, explains why a wider view of maritime risk is becoming increasingly important for operators and insurers navigating a more volatile trading environment. When traffic moves, exposure changes with it Hormuz and the Bosporus provide the clearest contrast in the data. The figures do not suggest a simple one-for-one movement of vessels from Hormuz to the Bosporus, but Pole Star’s analysis indicates the two shifts may be connected. Established patterns can change quickly when a major route becomes harder to use. The composition of that traffic matters too. Pole Star’s analysis suggests tankers account for a disproportionate share of the recent increase through the Bosporus, with some ownership structures, flag histories and transmission patterns consistent with shadow fleet activity. That does not explain the entire surge, but it does raise a wider question for operators and underwriters, where a sharp increase in volume may also bring a change in the type of vessels using a route and the risks attached to them. A diversion may reduce exposure to an immediate threat, but it can add time to a voyage, increase reliance on another constrained passage or place a vessel in a different operating environment. The Associated Press has reported on Gulf producers using alternative pipelines, shuttle services and ship-to-ship transfers to keep oil moving amid disruption around Hormuz. Cargo continues to move, but the routes and operating conditions around it can change considerably. Panama offers another version of the problem. Daily transits averaged 27.5 in 2024, during the El Niño drought restrictions, before recovering to more than 35 in 2026. Yet the underlying vulnerability remains. The Guardian has reported on renewed restrictions as drought and lower water levels put capacity under pressure again. Traffic volume only tells part of the story The quieter figures are revealing for a different reason. Pole Star’s research found that traffic through the Strait of Gibraltar rose from 186.8 in 2024 to 196.1 in 2026, an increase of 4.9%, while English Channel transits rose by 2.9%. Neither suggests a dramatic change in volume. Gibraltar illustrates why that can be deceptive. Pole Star’s behavioural analysis identified loitering and paired-vessel activity in the western approaches that could be consistent with attempts to obscure cargo origin, with tanker involvement higher than might be expected from the segment’s share of traffic. These patterns warrant closer scrutiny rather than proving wrongdoing in themselves, but they show why a stable headline number can sit alongside a changing risk picture. There is also the question of what cannot be seen. Pole Star’s transit analysis relies on vessel position reporting, so activity will be understated wherever vessels reduce or suspend transmissions. Hormuz and the Black Sea are among the areas where this matters most. The observed figures are therefore better understood as a floor than a complete total. For operators and insurers, raw transit numbers become much less useful when the available picture is incomplete or the make-up of traffic has changed beneath a broadly stable total. Building a fuller view of maritime risk Assessing that environment calls for more than a single stream of vessel data. AIS remains fundamental to maritime visibility, but its limitations become more important where transmissions are inconsistent. LRIT can provide another reference point, while satellite-derived observations can add context when reported movements and observed activity do not align. Used together, those sources provide a better basis for judging what a change actually means. Unusual movement may have an entirely routine explanation, while another pattern may justify closer scrutiny. The important part is having enough information to make that distinction with confidence. This matters most around chokepoints, where the picture can change quickly. Operators and insurers need to be able to see when normal patterns start to shift, and to check those changes against more than one source before making decisions on routing or exposure. articles.body: Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (K Line) has signed shipbuilding contracts with South Korea’s HD Hyundai Samho for two LPG dual-fuel very large gas carriers. The vessels are scheduled for delivery in 2030 and will each have cargo tank capacity of approximately 90,000 m³. Measuring around 230 metres in length and 32.25 metres in breadth, the new VLGCs will be capable of passing through both the old and new locks of the Panama Canal. According to K Line, the restricted beam will offer greater flexibility when determining Panama Canal transit arrangements in response to congestion, traffic restrictions and other operational conditions. The design is intended partly to support rising LPG export volumes from the United States. The vessels will feature dual-fuel engines capable of operating on LPG. Using LPG as marine fuel is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants compared with conventional fuel operation. In addition to LPG, the ships will be capable of carrying liquefied ammonia. K Line said the cargo flexibility was incorporated in anticipation of future demand for ammonia transportation as energy markets move towards lower-carbon alternatives. Through the two newbuildings, the Japanese shipping company plans to expand its VLGC fleet and strengthen its capacity to support the transportation and stable supply of liquefied gases. articles.body: LNG Bunker Snapshot: Europe’s supply worries lift ARA as Singapore falls in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 ARA Rotterdam’s LNG bunker price has risen in line with TTF. Front-month TTF has climbed by $1.05/MMBtu ($55/mt) to $29.64/MMBtu ($1,541/mt). Rotterdam’s bunker premium has edged up from $2.75/MMBtu ($143/mt) a week ago to $2.79/MMBtu ($145/mt), and the Baltic premium from $4.73/MMBtu ($246/mt) to $4.77/MMBtu ($248/mt). TTF has risen after easing a bit, when milder weather and a recovery in LNG availability held gas prices down, according to Rystad Energy gas and LNG senior analyst Ole Dramdal. European gas then jumped as supply worries resurfaced, with Norway keeping its Visund field shut for another month, until January, said ANZ Bank senior commodity strategist Daniel Hynes. Mounting Middle East tensions leave gas traders with little buffer if LNG shipments are disrupted further, Hynes added. LNG carrier transits through the Strait of Hormuz have averaged about 1.5 a day in November, and a further recovery would weigh on prices while renewed escalation could quickly reverse that, Rystad’s Dramdal added. EU gas storage withdrawals are running at their highest in a decade as LNG arrivals have slowed, leaving stocks 20%, or 18.5 billion cbm, below their five-year average, according to International Energy Agency (IEA) gas analyst Greg Molnár. Hormuz flows have recovered but remain well below pre-crisis levels, the IEA’s Molnár said, while LNG supply growth elsewhere has slowed as new projects take time to ramp up. China’s heating season began on 15 November, which could intensify competition for flexible LNG cargoes in the coming weeks, he added. Singapore Singapore’s LNG bunker price has fallen while ARA’s has risen, widening its discount to ARA from $41/mt a week ago to $168/mt. January JKM has fallen by $1.19/MMBtu ($62/mt) to $28.41/MMBtu ($1,478/mt). Singapore’s bunker premium has narrowed from $0.96/MMBtu ($50/mt) a week ago to $0.79/MMBtu ($41/mt), which has contributed $9/mt to the price decline. More US cargoes have headed to Europe, and some large Asian importers have bought less, ANZ Bank’s Hynes said. Asian spot demand has stayed soft as comfortable inventories limit buying, Rystad’s Dramdal said. China is expected to stay largely out of the market and South Korea is unlikely to step up purchases before the first quarter of 2027 in normal weather, while buyers in Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam have been active. In other LNG bunker news, Singapore’s LNG bunker sales fell by 3% to 50,000 mt in October, according to preliminary data from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. Cruise operator Carnival Corporation has ordered two dual-fuel cruise ships from Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri for delivery in 2033 and 2035, with LNG as the primary fuel, according to Fincantieri. Engine maker Everllence has won the first order for its latest methane dual-fuel engine, which will be fitted to two RoRo vessels ordered by Luxembourg-based logistics company Compagnie Luxembourgeoise de Navigation (CLdN). Maran Tankers Management, part of Greece’s Angelicoussis Group, has taken delivery of the sixth of eight LNG dual-fuel oil tankers being built at China’s New Times Shipbuilding.
