articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Red week by global sell-off in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index fell 9.91 points (4.56%) to close at 207.23, swept up in a broad global sell-off — the S&P 500 lost 8.61%, its worst week since April 2025, on a sharp shift in sentiment toward technology shares. The UPI fell less than the S&P, partly because its Asian constituents had already closed before the worst of the US session; the median dropped 5.24% and the weighted index (wUPI) 2.5%, on well-below-average volume. Only four names rose, led by ADNOC (+8.75%) rebounding off support toward its all-time highs, with Korea Line +2%, Nakilat just under 1% and COSCO +0.61%. The damage was led by Capital Clean Energy Carriers (−14.21%, breaking two support levels in the broad sell-off despite a strong Q3), with Excelerate (−11.13%) and Tsakos (−10.2%) also down double digits, and FLEX LNG (−9.73%) and Golar (−9.16%) closing behind. In the background, the gas market calmed: Asian and European prices both eased and converged near $26.8/MMBtu as Hormuz flows continued and Asian inventories stayed comfortable. Qatar kept signing US supply deals — potentially a quarter of new global supply by 2030 — and a new, likely non-oil-indexed Orlen contract is being drawn up to replace the terminated 2009 deal. Spot tanker rates fell to $20,000 (Atlantic) and $52,000 (Pacific). UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, lost 9.91 points (4.56%) to close at 207.23 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 8.61%. The chart below illustrates the performance of both indices with weekly data. Week 47-2026: Chart of the UP World LNG Shipping Index with S&P 500 (Source: UP-Indices) Broader View The UPI, like most equity markets, continued to fall, driven by a shift in sentiment towards technology shares. The chart shows that the S&P 500 index fell more sharply than the UPI. This is to some extent due to the UPI’s global scope, as Asian markets had already closed by the time the US trading session began. The median change was -5.24 per cent, whilst the weighted wUPI index fell by 2.5 per cent. Trading volume was well below average. In the LNG market, Qatar’s efforts to minimise losses and maximise potential continue. Qatar thus continued to sign contracts for US gas, with global Qatari supplies potentially accounting for a quarter of new global supplies by around 2030. Qatar is thus capitalising on what it does not offer its customers – the freedom to dispose of the gas they purchase as they see fit, i.e. the ability to change the final destination according to current market conditions. Qatari customers must unload the gas at the location they specified at the time of loading. Both Reuters and Bloomberg also reported on the background to the recent termination of the long-term contract between Poland’s Orlen and QatarEnergy: a new contract is being drawn up, in which the price of gas will likely no longer be linked to the price of oil, as was the case in the original 2009 contract. This is therefore not a matter of a loss of confidence in Qatari supplies, but primarily a question of price, with Orlen having invoked force majeure to suspend deliveries. The Reuters weekly round-up states that the situation on the gas market has calmed down over the past week. Prices fell for both Asia ($26.90 per MMBtu) and Europe ($26.75 per MMBtu). Thus, there was not only a fall in prices but also a levelling out. “Continued LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz and comfortable Asian inventories that limit spot buying interest are easing market pressures,” said Ole Dramdal, senior analyst at Rystad Energy. Some buying interest, however, was visible in South and South-East Asia, he said, with Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam showing buying interest. “In north-east Asia, buyers have stepped back from the spot market, with Chinese firms purchasing only enough to meet storage targets, South Korean buyers already covered for winter, and Japanese demand well supplied by long-term contracts,” said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus. “European LNG prices fell sharply over the week as improving global supply expectations and weak Asian competition outweighed tightening European winter fundamentals,” said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy, adding that US feedgas at near-record levels pointed to strong export availability from the Atlantic Basin. “Middle Eastern supply also continued its gradual recovery. Qatar and Abu Dhabi exported around one cargo per day during the first half of November.” Spot rates for LNG tankers fell to $20,000 for the Atlantic and $52,000 for the Pacific, according to Spark Commodities. Constituents In the previous paragraph, we mentioned the growth in exports through the Strait of Hormuz. This had a positive impact on ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADX: ADNOCLS), which posted the biggest gain of the past week: +8.75 per cent. It thus capitalised on the halt at the support level we mentioned, erasing several weeks’ worth of losses in a single week and returning to within striking distance of its all-time highs. The second-largest gain was recorded by Korea Line Corporation (KRX: 005880), which rose by two per cent and continues to trade sideways. NAKILAT (QSE: QGTS) rose by just under one per cent (UPI is calculated based on Friday’s prices). It thus maintained the price levels seen over the summer, when the ceasefire agreement was in place. The final gain was recorded by COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation (SS: 600026; +0.61 per cent). In its case, this represents a slowdown in the decline, though it is as yet difficult to judge how this will play out. As we have previously noted – and the situation remains unchanged – we are unsure whether this is a correction following a rise or a continuation of the downtrend. We’ll have a clearer picture once the price reaches 14 or 26 yuan. The declines are primarily linked to developments in the broader equity and commodities markets, which can be described as extraordinary. Nevertheless, the price levels reached allow us to assess and update the areas of interest to investors. The biggest fall of the week was seen in Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC; -14.21 per cent). The share price broke through two support levels in one go, thereby bringing the previous sideways trend to a decisive end. Although the price had already been in these regions earlier this year, it had never closed so low. And it certainly hadn’t fallen there so quickly. The drop looks sentiment- and valuation-driven within the broader sell-off; there was no company-specific news to explain its magnitude, and CCEC’s Q3 was in fact strong. Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE; -11.13 per cent) and Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN; -10.2 per cent) also fell by over ten per cent. Excelerate Energy ended its attempt at an uptrend by returning to a sideways range, whilst Tsakos broke below its autumn highs and entered the subsequent price range seen during the summer, giving it sufficient room to manoeuvre. Two companies with similar ticker symbols also fell by just under ten per cent: Flex LNG (NYSE: FLNG; -9.73 per cent) and Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG; -9.16 per cent). Flex cut through the $25 level like a knife through butter and closed a further two dollars lower. This now appears to be the optimal zone; after all, the annual dividend yield at these prices, with the nearest ex-date on 27 November, exceeds 12 per cent. EPS for the third (record-breaking) quarter covers this dividend. Paradoxically, a fall and a continued stay at this level even after the New Year could prompt management to adjust the dividend downwards, should they deem a dividend yield above 10 per cent to be too high. This could thus be a self-fulfilling prophecy, but one that would certainly stabilise the FLNG share price and restore its reputation as an equity bond. Golar’s share price looks similar; it too has returned to the range-bound trading seen in 2025 and 2026. Trading volume was well above average for both stocks, linked to support-level breaks and updated market sentiment. Another pair lost over six per cent: BP (NYSE: BP; -6.46 per cent) and Dynagas LNG Partners (NYSE: DLNG; -6.33 per cent). BP is in a congested zone, whilst Dynagas, despite solid quarterly results, dipped below its previous support level, as the weekly price action showed a narrow short-term sideways range. However, the price remained within the magnetic support formed by the shadow. No fewer than four companies fell by five per cent: ALNG (OSE: ALNG; -5.8 per cent), Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (TSE: 9104; -5.6 per cent), Shell (NYSE: SHEL; -5.55 per cent) and Chevron (NYSE: CVX; -5.24 per cent). ALNG continues to trade sideways following its quarterly results. Of particular interest is the signing of contracts for both tankers, which had previously been operating on the spot market. If we can expect a typical price, it could range between 50,000 and 75,000 dollars, although management emphasised, above all, a higher utilisation rate than the current 73 per cent. The core focus, however, remains the expansion of operations to include gas trading, on which there is as yet no new news. MOL, like the other two Japanese companies, has held its previous support level and thus retained scope for an upward move. Chevron is in a similar situation to BP, but Shell is now more akin to the Japanese trio. It has also held within a range from which, given favourable conditions, it can envisage growth somewhat more easily than BP and Chevron. NYK Line (TSE: 9101) and “K” Line (TSE: 9107), the remaining members of the Japanese trio, fell by around 4 per cent. Exmar (EBR: EXM) fell by 3.42 per cent and remains in a sideways trend. MISC (KLSE: 3816) lost 2 per cent; it remains near its support level, and only the reaction following the market open will reveal more. Pan Ocean (KRX: 028670) held steady at support, which roughly marks the low point of this year’s price movement. New Fortress Energy (NASDAQ: NFE) remained unchanged compared with the week before last, although it tested moves in both directions during the week. Crystal Ball Qatar remains on the sidelines among the losers of this conflict, yet its actions over the past few weeks have boosted market optimism, deepened by new U.S. contracts. Its efforts to honour its commitments and fulfil its orders are undoubtedly a significant boost to its customers. US producers are seeking to capitalise on the resulting vacuum by accelerating capacity expansion as supplier diversification takes place. Price is no longer the sole criterion, and even Bangladesh has announced that it has signed a long-term contract with a US producer. Whilst the coming winter months will bring increased uncertainty and a scramble for gas – partly due to the uncertain geopolitical situation, with a significant risk of further US strikes on Iran – we expect the situation to stabilise and adapt in the spring, primarily through the diversification of suppliers. Source: By Tomas Novotny, UP-Indices.com 2026-11-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Western Indian Ocean and Red Sea States advance regional maritime task force, elect first woman Chair in International Shipping News 24/11/2026 Signatory States to the Djibouti Code of Conduct and its Jeddah Amendment (DCoC/JA) have adopted a Regional Maritime Security Strategy and agreed to advance the establishment of a Combined Maritime Task Force (CMTF), at their Ninth High-Level Meeting in Antananarivo, Madagascar (11–13 November). The Meeting elected Ms. Stella Katondo, United Republic of Tanzania, as Chair, the first woman to lead the DCoC since its adoption in 2009. The Republic of South Africa will serve as Deputy Chair. The CMTF is intended to strengthen operational cooperation and coordination at sea among Signatory States, building on existing national capabilities and regional maritime security arrangements, to better counter piracy and protect seafarers. Signatory States agreed to develop its regional legal framework and Concept of Operations in 2027. The Regional Maritime Security Strategy covering the Western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden and Red Sea and based on the principle of “Maritime Security for a Purpose”, is supported by three related instruments also adopted: an Implementation Plan, a Risk Register and a Common Maritime Security Lexicon. Signatory States also committed to integrating women into all aspects of maritime security through the DCoC and its Working Groups. Mr. Mohamed Abdulkadir Mohamed, Minister of State of the Federal Republic of Somalia, highlighted the humanitarian dimension of maritime security, particularly the plight of seafarers affected by piracy and other attacks against commercial shipping. “The protection of seafarers is not simply a maritime security obligation; it is a fundamental humanitarian responsibility,” he said. The meeting brought together more than 100 representatives of Signatory States and international partners. It was convened by the DCoC/JA Steering Committee in collaboration with the IMO, the Indian Ocean Commission (IOC), the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) and the Government of Madagascar, with funding from the European Union through the Safe Seas for Africa Project. Source: IMO 2026-11-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Korean shipbuilding exports hit eight-year high, account for one-third of trade surplus in Shipbuilding News 24/11/2026 As South Korea achieved an annual export value of $1 trillion, domestic shipbuilders are also contributing to the effort. They are continuing their export growth by leading with eco-friendly and high-value-added vessels, such as liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers. According to industry sources on the 23rd, South Korea’s ship export value is projected to reach approximately $33.6 billion this year. Last year’s ship export value was approximately $31.8 billion, marking a record high in eight years. This follows a three-year consecutive increase from $21.8 billion in 2023 and $25.6 billion in 2024. It is also contributing to the improvement of the trade balance. Last year’s ship import value was approximately $4.6 billion, resulting in a trade surplus of approximately $27.2 billion. This accounts for 35% of South Korea’s total trade surplus (approximately $78 billion). In fact, among the 79th LNG carriers ordered worldwide up to mid-this month, the three major domestic shipbuilders (HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, and Samsung Heavy Industries) secured orders for 46 vessels. This accounts for approximately 58% of total orders. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Samsung Heavy Industries each secured 19 vessels, while Hanwha Ocean secured 8. They are also standing out in gas carriers that transport liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and ammonia. Up to last month, a total of 103 very large gas carriers (VLGCs) and very large ammonia carriers (VLACs) were ordered in the global market, of which the three major domestic shipbuilders secured 65 vessels (63.1%). In particular, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries secured orders for 53 vessels, accounting for 51.5%, more than half of the world’s order volume. Domestic shipbuilders are expanding their presence in the special vessel sector beyond merchant ships. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean have entered the U.S. Navy’s maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) business for warships, accumulating maintenance records for military support vessels and others. Hanwha Ocean plans to strengthen its local business based on the U.S. Philly Shipyard, while HD Hyundai Heavy Industries plans to do so through a joint venture with U.S. engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firm Keewat. They are also accelerating efforts to open new markets in preparation for the period after the shipbuilding boom and to respond to China’s pursuit. A representative area is power generation engines. This is because demand for power supply facilities is growing as artificial intelligence (AI) data center construction surges, centered on the United States. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries signed power equipment supply contracts with U.S.-based Aperion Energy Group for 627.1 billion won and Coban Energy Group for 956 billion won this year, respectively. In the marine sector, development of floating data centers (FDCs) and floating power generation facilities (BMPPs) is in full swing. Samsung Heavy Industries is promoting a 50-megawatt-class floating data center project with a U.S. company, while Hanwha Ocean is collaborating with global power and automation firm ABB. Small modular reactors (SMRs) are also an area that domestic shipbuilders are focusing on as a future growth driver. Following its $30 million investment in U.S. next-generation nuclear power company TerraPower in 2022, HD Hyundai is expanding its nuclear equipment business by securing orders for reactor vessel manufacturing. Samsung Heavy Industries is accelerating the development of floating nuclear power plants that mount SMRs on offshore floating bodies, partnering with the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, U.S. nuclear design firm Sargent & Lundy (S&L), and others. An industry official said, “While continuing export growth centered on high-value-added vessels, we will secure additional export momentum in new businesses.” Source: MoneyToday 2026-11-24 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

It expects to procure the work in December. The university wants a company specialising in ship production design to carry out the work. Production design is the stage that turns a vessel concept into the detailed drawings a shipyard builds from. The university described the notice as a preliminary plan, with the final terms to follow in formal tender documents. The notice does not say who will own or operate the vessel or where it will bunker. Methanol bunker supply is already growing in Zhejiang. Petroleum products company China Marine Bunker (PetroChina) took delivery of a methanol bunker vessel in Zhoushan in June. A methanol delivery at Ningbo-Zhoushan’s Meishan terminal set a record as the largest single methanol bunker operation in the province, according to the port authority. articles.body: Korea, U.S. Seek Faster Energy and Shipbuilding Cooperation as Seoul Urges Visa Reforms in Shipbuilding News 24/11/2026 South Korea’s Second Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs, Kim Ji-na, who is visiting the United States, emphasized the urgent need for regulatory improvements and changes to the U.S. visa system to achieve tangible results in bilateral economic cooperation. Vice Minister Kim delivered a keynote address at the 10th U.S.-ROK Joint Public-Private Economic Forum, held at the Hudson Institute in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17 (local time), proposing faster cooperation in the energy and shipbuilding sectors. She stressed the need to streamline approval procedures and facilitate the movement of experts and skilled technical personnel through improvements to the visa system, calling on the U.S. government and Congress for support. She also urged the creation of a favorable investment environment, including investment incentives and legislative support, to facilitate Korean companies’ investments in the United States and the implementation of strategic investment projects. Kim further emphasized the need to deliver concrete results from strategic investments in energy, including power infrastructure for artificial intelligence and nuclear energy. At the forum, differences emerged between officials from the two countries over South Korea’s network usage fee policy. Arielle Roth, U.S. Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information and Administrator of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), criticized South Korea’s network usage fee system as unique in the world, arguing that it runs counter to bilateral plans for next-generation 6G cooperation. In response, Lee Ji-yoon, Deputy Director-General for International Economic Affairs, countered that the Korean government aims to create an environment in which all companies can compete on fair terms. She explained that the measure is intended to build trust in online platform operations by ensuring fair competition in the digital market. She added that discussions on digital-related legislation in South Korea are also aimed at ensuring a level playing field in the digital market. Vice Minister Kim outlined the $350 billion U.S. investment plan, citing cooperation on a gas-fired power plant in Texas and nuclear energy projects. However, she made no mention of the Alaska liquefied natural gas (LNG) project, into which U.S. President U.S. President Donald Trump said that $50 billion of South Korea’s investment would be directed toward the project. The Korean government has maintained a cautious stance, saying it will decide whether to invest after conducting a feasibility review. Elizabeth Urbanas, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Asia and the Americas in the Department of Energy’s Office of International Affairs, who attended the forum, stressed the importance of turning the projects and investment plans into concrete results. U.S. Senator Bill Hagerty, speaking at the closing session, proposed prioritizing the implementation of South Korea’s U.S. investment plan, including purchase agreements for the Alaska LNG pipeline project and expansion of the U.S. shipbuilding industry. Wendy Cutler, former deputy U.S. trade representative, acknowledged that some had viewed the pace of South Korean investment as falling short of expectations, but said it appeared to be getting back on track, potentially easing those concerns. The forum also addressed specific areas of cooperation in energy and shipbuilding. The first session covered bilateral energy projects and ways to build supply chains to ensure stable access to key resources, including critical minerals. In the second session, major South Korean shipbuilders presented their current U.S. operations and future plans, while participants explored policy and legislative support measures to accelerate bilateral shipbuilding cooperation. A third session examined broader challenges in bilateral economic cooperation, including discussions on digital-related legislation. Former senior officials offered differing assessments of prospects for U.S.-North Korea talks and broader security issues. Former U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell said that recognizing North Korea as a nuclear-armed state would serve neither South Korea’s nor the United States’ interests, addressing the possibility of President Trump pursuing a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Joseph Yun, former U.S. Special Representative for North Korea policy, said North Korea was unlikely to rush into talks, given the stronger position it has gained through cooperation with Russia. Following the forum, Vice Minister Kim held a separate meeting with Senator Hagerty, again seeking congressional support to facilitate the entry and stay of South Korean business personnel in the United States and advance bilateral shipbuilding cooperation. The forum brought together approximately 50 participants, including government officials from both countries, business representatives and think tank experts, to discuss economic security and industrial strength. articles.body: Europe Offshore North Sea decommissioning spending set to hit $32bn by 2035 Bojan Lepic November 24, 2026 0 694 1 minute read HSD HSD Oil and gas companies operating in the UK North Sea are expected to spend £24.7bn ($32.5bn) on decommissioning over the next decade, according to a new report from industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK). The organisation’s latest decommissioning outlook forecasts expenditure between 2026 and 2035, with annual spending expected to peak at approximately £3.1bn ($4bn) in 2027. Spending is projected to remain above £2.7bn ($3.52bn) annually through 2031 as operators proceed with well abandonment, platform removal, and subsea infrastructure recovery. The programme includes decommissioning 1,834 wells and removing 135 platform topsides and 126 subsea structures. The central North Sea is expected to account for approximately 56% of total expenditure during the period. OEUK warned that the growing workload could create competition for specialist vessels, engineering capacity, ports and skilled workers, particularly as offshore wind construction accelerates. The organisation expects new UK offshore wind capacity additions to peak at around 5.2GW in 2029, increasing pressure on some of the same marine construction and installation resources required for decommissioning. The report also highlights that 71% of the value of decommissioning contracts awarded during 2025 went to UK-based companies. According to the North Sea Transition Authority, the estimated remaining cost of decommissioning the entire UK offshore oil and gas sector stands at approximately £43.4bn ($56.6bn). OEUK called for better coordination between operators and earlier contracting commitments to avoid bottlenecks and keep more work within the UK supply chain. articles.summary: Engen-led consortium’s proposed LNG-to-power project features a 1.9 GW power plant, LNG import terminal, and related infrastructure.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects November 24, 2026 · 1 minute ago $2.3 billion integrated LNG-to-power project on the development agenda in South Africa Engen-led consortium’s proposed LNG-to-power project features a 1.9 GW power plant, LNG import terminal, and related infrastructure. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Durban LNG site Source: VTTI A proposed ZAR 40 billion ($2.3 billion) liquefied natural gas (LNG)-to-power development project in Durban has the potential to boost South Africa's energy security, with an Engen-led consortium reaffirming plans to develop an LNG import terminal, pipeline network, and 1.9 GW combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power plant targeted for operation in 2031, which could generate enough electricity to supply the equivalent of 3.9 million households. An Engen-led consortium has confirmed its plans to develop an integrated LNG-to-power project, comprising an LNG import terminal, associated pipeline infrastructure and a 1.9 GW combined cycle gas turbine power plant in the Durban area, with the LNG terminal situated in the Port of Durban and the power plant developed at the Engen refinery site, which is currently being converted into a fuel import storage facility. This project would provide a reliable source of gas to industrial users across KwaZulu-Natal. The consortium brings together international companies, including VTTI , a provider of energy infrastructure solutions, which would develop and operate the LNG terminal and pipeline infrastructure. Vitol , an energy and commodities company, would supply the LNG, while Saudi-listed Acwa , said to be the world’s largest private water desalination company engaged in energy transition and green hydrogen at scale, would develop the power plant. The LNG-to-power project, which targets approximately 30% ownership by South African Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) partners, is expected to enter into the construction phase in late 2028, subject to a final investment decision (FID) and necessary local approvals, with the power plant targeted to begin operations in H2 2031. The project is anticipated to support approximately 4,500 person-years of employment across the South African economy during construction, with up to around 1,000 workers on site at peak, and approximately 740 ongoing jobs during operations, of which around 220 would be direct. The construction phase is estimated to contribute approximately ZAR 26 billion ($1.49 billion) to South African GDP, and ongoing operations approximately ZAR 1.8 billion ($103.3 million) per year. The LNG terminal would have a peak regasification capacity of around 5 billion cubic meters per annum, helping South Africa respond to the anticipated decline in pipeline gas imports from Mozambique as production from existing gas fields decreases. Aside from supplying gas to the proposed 1.9 GW power plant, the terminal would provide reliable gas supplies to industrial users, which could support the development of a lower-carbon energy and industrial hub in Durban, unlock investment in new industries, and help enable the development of energy-intensive infrastructure such as data centres. The preliminary estimates indicate that the project is expected to generate more than ZAR 245 million ($14.1 million) per year in throughput-related revenue for the Port of Durban and could provide the LNG infrastructure required to offer LNG bunkering services to visiting vessels. " Reliable energy supply underpins economic growth. Engen is delighted to be part of a project which could deliver energy to industry and power 3.9 million households. We look forward to working with our partners and stakeholders to deliver energy solutions to South Africa. " — George Roberts Managing Director and CEO of Engen and EVP South for Vivo Energy The project’s development remains subject to participation in South Africa’s second gas-to-power procurement round, the receipt of all relevant regulatory and environmental approvals, and the achievement of other key project milestones. articles.body: Asia Operations Shipyards Seatrium cuts 220 jobs in latest post-merger restructuring Bojan Lepic November 24, 2026 0 811 1 minute read Seatrium Seatrium Singapore-based offshore and marine engineering group Seatrium is laying off around 220 employees, representing 2% of its local workforce, as part of a restructuring programme to streamline operations and consolidate its global shipyard network. The move marks the company’s first formal workforce restructuring exercise since the 2023 merger of Sembcorp Marine and Keppel Offshore & Marine. Seatrium said it was accelerating the reorganisation of its Singapore facilities under its One Seatrium Global Delivery Model, which allocates projects across its international yards based on capacity and resources. The company has already reduced its global yard network from 15 facilities in 2023 to 11. Tuas Boulevard Yard will remain its flagship mega-yard, while Admiralty Yard, which has been progressively scaled down, will be returned to the Singapore government in 2028. Operations at Benoi, Pioneer and Tuas yards will be refocused, with Tuas Yard concentrating on higher-value repairs and upgrades. Seatrium chief executive Chris Ong said the changes were intended to position the company for future growth rather than simply reduce costs. The company said it had explored redeployment and retraining opportunities before proceeding with the redundancies. Affected employees will receive retrenchment packages and employment assistance through the Seatrium Employees Union and Singapore’s labour movement. The restructuring comes just days after Seatrium reported a net order book of S$12.2bn ($9.45bn), covering 35 projects with deliveries extending into 2033. The group secured S$1.7bn ($1.32bn) in new orders during 2026 and expects underlying full-year net profit to be materially higher than in 2025, supported by improving margins and project execution. articles.body: Danaos Corporation reported higher revenue and earnings for the third quarter of 2026, supported by increased contributions from both its containership and dry bulk operations. The Greek shipowner generated operating revenue of US$284.3 million during the three months ended 30 September 2026, up 9% from US$260.7 million in the corresponding period of 2025. Net income increased to US$176.2 million from US$130.6 million a year earlier, while diluted earnings per share rose to US$9.64 from US$7.11. Adjusted net income reached US$152.1 million, equivalent to US$8.32 per diluted share, compared with US$124.1 million and US$6.75 per share in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA increased to US$207.3 million from US$181.6 million. Danaos’ containership segment generated US$247.8 million in operating revenue during the quarter, compared with US$239.1 million a year earlier. Revenue from dry bulk vessels rose to US$36.5 million from US$21.6 million. Adjusted EBITDA from the containership business increased to US$179.7 million, while the dry bulk segment contributed US$22.4 million, more than double the US$9.1 million reported in the same quarter last year. Containership utilisation reached 99.6%, compared with 98.1% in the third quarter of 2025. The company operated an average of 76.3 containerships and 11 dry bulk vessels during the reporting period. Danaos said it added approximately US$611 million to its contracted revenue backlog through new charters and extensions agreed since its previous earnings release. Total contracted operating revenue now stands at US$5 billion, including newbuildings, with an average remaining containership charter duration of 4.5 years. Charter coverage currently stands at 100% for 2026, 94% for 2027, 84% for 2028, 71% for 2029 and 53% for 2030. “The container market continued to strengthen and the liner companies reported strong third-quarter results. Open tonnage remains scarce and the charter market has strengthened with it,” said Dr John Coustas, Chief Executive Officer of Danaos. “We used those conditions to add approximately US$611 million to our contracted revenue backlog, which now stands at US$5 billion,” he added. During the third quarter, Danaos took delivery of three 8,258 TEU newbuildings: Santorini Express, Tinos Express and Patmos Express. All three vessels commenced five-year charters following delivery. The company also added two 9,000 TEU containerships to its orderbook, with delivery scheduled for the first quarter of 2029. Danaos’ containership orderbook now comprises 28 vessels with an aggregate capacity of 177,776 TEU. Fifteen vessels are scheduled for delivery in 2027, seven in 2028 and six in 2029. Its dry bulk orderbook includes four 211,000 dwt Newcastlemax vessels scheduled for delivery in 2028. On a fully delivered basis and assuming no vessel disposals, Danaos’ fleet would comprise 106 containerships with an aggregate capacity of approximately 680,000 TEU and 15 dry bulk vessels totalling around 2.8 million dwt. The company has meanwhile deferred its proposed carve-out and sale of a minority stake in its dry bulk division through the Norwegian market. Danaos said it continues to consider the transaction a potential option but intends to pursue it only when market conditions support optimal shareholder value. At the end of September, Danaos held US$1.06 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Gross debt stood at US$1.38 billion, resulting in a net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA ratio of 0.43 times.

articles.body: Business Developments & Projects November 24, 2026 · 1 minute ago Germany secures 18-year supply of Norwegian gas with Equinor-VNG deal This is Equinor’s longest deal since 1986 and entails the supply of natural gas to Germany from 2027 through 2044. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Anders Opedal (left), President and CEO of Equinor, and Ulf Heitmüller, CEO of VNG Credit: Ole Jørgen Bratland/Equinor Norwegian state-owned energy giant Equinor has locked in a multi-year natural gas supply agreement with German energy company VNG, committing to deliver up to 1.4 billion cubic meters (bcm) of gas annually from January 2027 through the end of 2044 and reinforcing Norway’s role in supporting Germany’s long-term energy security. Equinor has signed an 18-year agreement to supply natural gas to VNG until the end of 2044, which will enable it to deliver up to 15.3 TWh, or around 1.4 billion cubic meters, of natural gas per year to the German company. Deliveries are scheduled to start on January 1, 2027, and continue until the end of 2044, with gas delivered at Trading Hub Europe, the German gas market area. The Norwegian giant has explained that the pricing will reflect market terms, while other commercial details are confidential between the two firms. This deal is deemed to be the longest gas sales agreement since the Troll ones were signed in 1986. VNG sees the agreement as a significant milestone in securing long-term gas supplies for customers in Germany. The two companies have a relationship dating back several decades, as the first natural gas deliveries from Norway to eastern Germany took place in 1996, so the new agreement builds on this established cooperation. " This milestone agreement with VNG demonstrates the continued demand for long-term gas supplies in Europe. Building on our long-standing partnership and reliable production from the Norwegian Continental Shelf, Equinor is well positioned to meet this demand and contribute to Europe’s energy security for years to come. " — Anders Opedal President and Chief Executove Officer (CEO) of Equinor The agreement between VNG Handel & Vertrieb (VNG H&V), a wholly owned subsidiary of VNG, and Equinor was signed in Oslo on November 24 by Ulf Heitmüller , Chair of the Executive Board of VNG, and Anders Opedal , President and CEO of Equinor. Germany is perceived to be the Norwegian player’s largest market for natural gas and has been an anchor market for gas from Norway since exports started in 1977. " — Ulf Heitmüller CEO of VNG According to Equinor, natural gas is expected to remain a key part of Europe’s energy mix as more renewable power and low-carbon gases are developed. The company emphasizes that Norwegian gas production is among the lowest-emission operations in the international gas industry. The firm also points out that pipeline supply from the Norwegian Continental Shelf benefits from electrification of platforms and onshore processing plants combined with short transport distances to the continent. articles.title: Circle Group launches MasterSPED 10.4 for integrated freight management
articles.summary: Circle Group has released MasterSPED 10.4, an updated software platform designed to bring freight forwarding, customs operations and accounting into a single workflow. Developed by NEXT Freight, the new version introduces additional automation tools for shipment management, financial administration and customs...
articles.body: Circle Group has released MasterSPED 10.4, an updated software platform designed to bring freight forwarding, customs operations and accounting into a single workflow. Developed by NEXT Freight, the new version introduces additional automation tools for shipment management, financial administration and customs documentation. The platform provides a unified dashboard covering sea, road and air freight, allowing logistics operators to monitor shipments and departmental activities through one interface. New customs and accounting capabilities One of the main changes is an upgraded accounting module that automatically records supplier invoices and matches them with shipment-related costs. The system also provides visibility into shipment profitability from the moment a shipment file is opened. Additional functions cover financial reporting and Intrastat submissions, including the use of digital signatures. For customs operations, MasterSPED 10.4 automatically retrieves TARIC data from the Italian Customs and Monopolies Agency (ADM). It can also generate DAU and DAT documents and incorporate them into administrative workflows. The release introduces cloud-based document management and real-time tracking of movements within transit warehouses using radio-frequency technology. Circle Group said the infrastructure upgrade also forms part of its efforts to align with the requirements of the European Union’s NIS2 Directive. Integration with MILOS Synapse and AI development MasterSPED 10.4 connects with MILOS Synapse, Circle Group’s orchestration platform introduced in September 2026. The integration allows MasterSPED to exchange information with other group solutions, including MILOS Global Supply Chain Visibility, MILOS TFP and MILOS TOS, as well as third-party systems. Circle Group is also developing AI agents capable of reading and interpreting documents received by email. This work is currently being conducted through a Proof of Concept. Another development area focuses on processing customer quotation requests through email exchanges. “With MasterSPED® 10.4, we offer a product that brings operations, customs and administration together in a single workflow,” said Luca Abatello, CEO of Circle Group. The company has not announced specific customer deployments or performance results associated with the new release.

articles.summary: Spain will ban wastewater discharges from ship exhaust gas cleaning systems, commonly known as scrubbers, in its ports and internal waters beginning July 1, 2027, imposing restrictions that go beyond...

Join the leading maritime news network ImagineStock / Shutterstock Spain will ban wastewater discharges from ship exhaust gas cleaning systems, commonly known as scrubbers, in its ports and internal waters beginning July 1, 2027, imposing restrictions that go beyond existing regional environmental requirements. The measure, established under Royal Decree 1006/2026 and published November 20, applies to all civilian vessels regardless of flag. It covers discharges from open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid scrubber systems in Spanish internal waters, port areas and designated anchorages. Scrubbers allow ships to meet International Maritime Organization (IMO) sulfur emissions limits while continuing to burn higher-sulfur fuel oil. However, the systems can generate wastewater containing heavy metals, hydrocarbons and other pollutants. The new rules implement a 2025 decision by the OSPAR Commission, which oversees marine environmental protection in the Northeast Atlantic. That agreement requires participating countries to prohibit open-loop scrubber discharges in ports and internal waters by July 2027, with restrictions extending to all scrubber operating modes by July 2029. Spain has chosen to accelerate the broader prohibition by two years and extend it nationwide, including to Mediterranean ports outside the OSPAR region. The ban does not prohibit scrubber use or apply across all Spanish territorial waters. Instead, vessels must stop discharging wastewater before entering restricted areas, either switching to compliant low-sulfur fuel or retaining wastewater onboard where technically possible. Spain already restricts scrubber discharges at several major ports, including Algeciras, Barcelona, Cartagena and Valencia. The decree establishes a common national standard. Spanish shipowners’ association ANAVE has criticized the accelerated timetable and broader geographic scope, calling for greater alignment with IMO guidelines. In its statement, ANAVE questioned whether Spain had adequately justified the additional restrictions through environmental risk assessments. It also raised concerns about the availability of port reception facilities for wastewater from closed-loop systems. The association noted that shipowners have invested heavily in scrubber technology under existing international regulations and warned against measures that undermine regulatory certainty. The decree also introduces reporting and inspection requirements. Scrubber-equipped ships must notify Spanish authorities of their systems at least 24 hours before arrival, or upon departure from the previous port for shorter voyages. Authorities may inspect fuel-changeover records and scrubber operating logs. Spain’s move reflects growing pressure to restrict scrubber wastewater discharges even as the technology remains an accepted method of meeting IMO air pollution standards. U.S. Central Command/Handout via REUTERS The U.S. Treasury Department on Monday announced new sanctions targeting financial networks supporting Iran’s oil exports and tanker operations, including companies accused of facilitating payments for the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC) and shipping arrangements linked to the Iranian military. The latest action , announced under Operation Economic Outcast, targets 22 entities and eight individuals involved in moving billions of dollars through Iran’s international financial networks. Unlike previous sanctions rounds focused on tankers and shipping companies, the latest measures target the financial infrastructure that allows Iran to collect oil revenues and pay for maritime services despite U.S. restrictions. Among those designated is Dubai-based OGA Global General Trading LLC, which Treasury said facilitated millions of dollars in payments for NITC, Iran’s state-owned tanker operator. Treasury also identified a tanker chartering arrangement involving the SERENE I (IMO 9197832). According to the department, Dubai-based H N B Trading Co LLC facilitated payment for the vessel’s charter involving Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company, an Iranian military-linked entity, and sanctioned shipping company Dragon Road Ltd. Other targets include Dubai-based Gespl International General Trading LLC, accused of facilitating oil and petrochemical sales for the National Iranian Oil Company, and Integral Petro Energy Trading LLC, which allegedly facilitated millions of dollars in liquefied petroleum gas sales involving Kharg Petrochemical Company. The sanctions also target the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which Treasury described as a central mechanism for connecting Iranian exporters earning foreign currency with importers seeking funds for overseas purchases. The institution reportedly supports tens of billions of dollars in annual trade, including transactions using Chinese yuan and Russian rubles. The action comes just days after Treasury claimed that no Iranian oil had been loaded onto vessels since Operation Economic Outcast began on August 24 and that no Iranian oil remained afloat outside the U.S. military blockade. Under U.S. sanctions rules, assets belonging to designated entities within U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, while foreign financial institutions may face additional sanctions exposure for facilitating certain transactions involving those entities.
